symptoms: may be detected only on routine BP measurement
guidance: Hypertension is a major risk factor for heart disease, stroke, and kidney disease. Lifestyle modifications: reduce salt intake (<5g/day), maintain healthy weight, regular exercise (30 min/day), limit alcohol, and stop smoking. Medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, CCBs, diuretics) are prescribed based on severity. BP should be monitored regularly at home or at PHCs. Free BP screening and medications are available at government NCD clinics.
precautions: Do not stop blood pressure medication without doctor's advice—even if you feel fine
Reduce salt intake (avoid pickles, papad, processed foods)
Exercise regularly (brisk walking for 30 minutes daily)
Monitor BP at home regularly and maintain a log
Seek emergency care for sudden severe headache, chest pain, or vision changes

symptoms: tingling or numbness in hands and feet
recurrent skin or urinary tract infections
guidance: Manage blood sugar through diet (high-fiber foods like ragi, whole wheat, vegetables; avoid refined sugar and white rice), regular exercise (30-45 min daily), and prescribed oral antidiabetics or insulin. Monitor blood sugar (fasting and postprandial) and HbA1c every 3-6 months. Free diabetes care and medicines are available at PHCs under the National Programme for Prevention and Control of NCDs. Annual foot, eye, and kidney checkups are essential to prevent complications.
precautions: Avoid sugary drinks, sweets, white bread, and polished white rice
Do not skip meals—maintain regular meal timing
Check feet daily for any wounds or sores (do not walk barefoot)
Take medications consistently—do not stop without consulting
Get annual eye exams (retinopathy screening) and kidney function tests

guidance: Type 1 diabetes requires lifelong insulin therapy. Multiple daily injections (basal-bolus) or insulin pump. Blood glucose monitoring 4-6 times daily. Learn to recognize and treat hypoglycemia (give 15g fast sugar: juice, glucose tablets). HbA1c should be checked every 3 months. Insulin and testing strips are available free at government hospitals. Sick-day management is essential—never skip insulin even if not eating.
precautions: Always carry fast-acting sugar (glucose tablets, juice) for hypoglycemic episodes
Do not skip insulin doses—this leads to DKA, a life-threatening emergency
Wear a medical alert ID
Monitor blood glucose before driving
Learn sick-day rules (check ketones, stay hydrated, call doctor)

symptoms: chest pain or pressure (angina) that occurs with exertion or stress
pain radiating to left arm, jaw, neck, or back
angina usually subsides with rest or nitroglycerin
guidance: CAD is caused by atherosclerotic plaque in coronary arteries. Management: lifestyle—heart-healthy diet (low saturated fat, high fiber), regular exercise, smoking cessation, and stress reduction. Medications: aspirin, statins, beta-blockers, and ACE inhibitors. For severe disease, angioplasty with stenting or coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG). Free cardiac care is available under PMJAY (Ayushman Bharat) at empanelled hospitals. Regular cardiology follow-up is essential.
precautions: Take aspirin daily if prescribed (unless contraindicated)
Do not smoke
Maintain a healthy weight and control BP/blood sugar
Know the signs of a heart attack—seek emergency care immediately if chest pain persists >20 min
Carry sublingual nitroglycerin as prescribed

symptoms: shortness of breath (dyspnea) on exertion or at rest
orthopnea (shortness of breath when lying flat)
paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking up gasping for air)
guidance: Heart failure is a chronic condition where the heart cannot pump enough blood. Management: medications (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics, aldosterone antagonists), fluid and salt restriction, daily weight monitoring, and regular exercise as tolerated. Implantable devices (CRT, ICD) in severe cases. Free care under PMJAY. Monitor for worsening symptoms (increased edema, weight gain, breathlessness).
precautions: Restrict salt intake (<2g/day) and fluid intake (as advised)
Weigh yourself daily—report weight gain >2 kg in 3 days
Take diuretics as prescribed—do not skip
Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) which worsen heart failure
Seek care for worsening breathlessness, orthopnea, or edema

symptoms: may be asymptomatic and detected incidentally
risk of stroke (clots in the heart go to the brain)
guidance: Atrial fibrillation is a common arrhythmia. Management: rate control (beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers) or rhythm control (antiarrhythmics, cardioversion). Anticoagulation (warfarin, DOACs) is critical to prevent stroke—the CHA₂DS₂-VASc score guides this. Free anticoagulants available at government hospitals. Regular ECG and follow-up with a cardiologist are essential.
precautions: Take anticoagulants exactly as prescribed to prevent stroke
Do not stop blood thinners without doctor's advice
Report any signs of bleeding (blood in urine/stool, bruising, nosebleeds)
Limit alcohol intake—can trigger AF
Monitor heart rate at home—report persistent >100/min

symptoms: history of acute rheumatic fever in childhood
guidance: RHD is a preventable complication of untreated strep throat. Secondary prophylaxis with monthly benzathine penicillin injections is essential to prevent recurrence and valve damage—free under government programs. In severe valve disease, surgery (valve repair/replacement) is needed. Free cardiac surgery under PMJAY. Avoid dental procedures without antibiotic prophylaxis.
precautions: Do not miss monthly penicillin injections—this prevents worsening
Inform dentists about RHD—need antibiotic prophylaxis for procedures
If breathlessness worsens, see a cardiologist
Monitor for signs of infective endocarditis (fever, new murmur)
Avoid high-salt diets and fluid overload

symptoms: may be idiopathic, post-viral, alcoholic, or familial
guidance: DCM is characterized by an enlarged, weakened heart. Treatment: heart failure medications (ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers, diuretics), lifestyle changes (salt restriction, fluid restriction), and avoidance of alcohol. In severe cases, ICD or cardiac transplant. Regular follow-up with echocardiography. Free care at government cardiology centers.
precautions: Strictly avoid alcohol
Monitor daily weight
Limit salt and fluid intake
Take medications consistently
Seek emergency care if palpitations or syncope occurs

symptoms: sudden cardiac death (risk in young athletes)
guidance: HCM is a genetic heart muscle disease. Management: avoid strenuous exercise and dehydration. Medications: beta-blockers, verapamil, or disopyramide. In severe obstructive cases, septal myectomy or alcohol septal ablation. ICD for high-risk (family history of sudden death, syncope, severe hypertrophy). Genetic counseling for family members.
precautions: Avoid intense physical exertion and competitive sports
Stay well-hydrated—avoid dehydration
If you have a family history of HCM, get screened
Report any episodes of dizziness or fainting immediately
Do not miss cardiology follow-ups

symptoms: leg pain or cramping when walking (intermittent claudication)
cold feet, pale or blue skin
non-healing ulcers or sores on feet/legs
absent or weak pulses in legs
hair loss on legs and feet
guidance: PAD is caused by atherosclerosis in leg arteries. Management: smoking cessation (most important), exercise (supervised walking program), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin/clopidogrel), statins, and strict control of diabetes/BP. Angioplasty or bypass surgery in severe cases. Free care at government hospitals. Regular foot care is essential to prevent amputation.
precautions: Stop smoking immediately
Walk daily (start slowly and increase) until pain starts, rest, repeat
Check feet daily for wounds—do not walk barefoot
Take aspirin and statins as prescribed
Seek emergency if leg becomes suddenly pale, cold, or painful (acute ischemia)

symptoms: transient ischemic attacks (TIA): temporary weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking
amaurosis fugax (temporary vision loss in one eye)
guidance: Carotid stenosis is a major stroke risk. Treatment: medical (antiplatelet, statin, BP control). For severe stenosis (>70%), carotid endarterectomy or stenting is recommended. Lifestyle changes: smoking cessation, healthy diet, exercise. Free surgical care under PMJAY.
precautions: Do not smoke
Control BP and cholesterol
If you have TIA symptoms (sudden weakness, speech difficulty), seek emergency—do not wait
Take antiplatelet medications as prescribed
Follow up with vascular surgeon or neurologist

symptoms: hemiparesis (weakness on one side of body)
guidance: Rehabilitation is key: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and swallowing training. Prevention of recurrence: antiplatelets/anticoagulants, BP control, statins, and diabetes management. Supportive care and caregiver education. Free rehabilitation at government hospitals under RBSK and NCD programs. Home modifications for safety (grab bars, ramps).
precautions: Do physical therapy daily to prevent contractures
Use swallow precautions (pureed food, sitting upright) to prevent aspiration pneumonia
Monitor BP regularly—tight control prevents recurrence
If depression occurs, seek psychiatric help
Modify home environment to prevent falls (remove trip hazards, install railings)

symptoms: swelling (edema) of ankles, feet, and face
guidance: CKD is progressive and often caused by diabetes or hypertension. Management: strict BP control (<130/80), blood sugar control, low-protein, low-salt, low-potassium diet. Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs). Free dialysis (hemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis) is available under the Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme (PMNDP) at district hospitals. Regular monitoring of creatinine, eGFR, and electrolytes. Consider renal transplant for eligible patients.
precautions: Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac) and other nephrotoxic drugs
Limit salt, potassium (bananas, oranges, potatoes), and phosphorus (dairy, nuts)
Monitor fluid intake as advised
Take prescribed medications (BP drugs, phosphate binders, erythropoietin) consistently
If on dialysis, adhere to the schedule strictly

guidance: Chronic GN is inflammation of the glomeruli. Treatment depends on the type: immunosuppressants (steroids, cyclophosphamide) for immune-mediated GN, BP control with ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and dietary modifications (salt/protein restriction). Regular monitoring of renal function and urine protein. Free immunosuppressants at government hospitals. Dialysis or transplant in end-stage.
precautions: Take immunosuppressants exactly as prescribed—do not stop abruptly
Monitor BP and urine protein regularly
Avoid high-salt and high-protein diets
Report any infection promptly (may reactivate GN)
If swelling or decreased urine, seek care

symptoms: may be associated with vesicoureteral reflux or obstruction
guidance: Chronic pyelonephritis results from recurrent renal infections. Treatment: long-term antibiotics for suppressive therapy (under specialist). Treat underlying causes: VUR, kidney stones, or obstruction. Hydration and good hygiene. Imaging (ultrasound, CT) to assess scarring. Monitor renal function.
precautions: Complete full antibiotic courses for UTIs
Drink plenty of water
Maintain good personal hygiene
If you have recurrent UTIs, a urologist should evaluate for anatomical issues
Monitor BP and renal function regularly

symptoms: shortness of breath, especially on exertion
history of smoking or biomass fuel exposure
guidance: COPD is largely preventable by avoiding smoking and biomass smoke. Management: smoking cessation (most important), inhalers (bronchodilators and corticosteroids), pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen therapy for severe cases, and annual flu and pneumococcal vaccinations. Free inhalers and oxygen therapy are available at government hospitals. Avoid dust, smoke, and air pollution.
precautions: Stop smoking completely
Use clean cooking fuel (LPG) under Ujjwala Yojana
Learn proper inhaler technique—use a spacer
Take prescribed inhalers daily—do not use only when symptoms worsen
Get annual flu and pneumococcal vaccines

symptoms: chronic productive cough with copious purulent sputum
guidance: Bronchiectasis is permanent dilation of airways. Treatment: chest physiotherapy (postural drainage), inhaled bronchodilators, mucolytics, and antibiotics for exacerbations. Manage underlying causes (e.g., immunodeficiency, CF). In severe cases, surgery or lung transplant. Smoking cessation is essential.
precautions: Perform chest physiotherapy daily
Stay well-hydrated to thin secretions
Avoid smoking and respiratory irritants
Complete antibiotic courses during exacerbations
Monitor for hemoptysis—seek care if severe

guidance: IPF is a progressive scarring of the lungs. Treatment: antifibrotic drugs (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow progression—available at government hospitals for eligible patients. Oxygen therapy for hypoxemia. Pulmonary rehabilitation. Lung transplant for suitable candidates. Avoid smoking and GERD (gastroesophageal reflux worsens).
precautions: Take antifibrotic medications as prescribed
Avoid smoking and secondhand smoke
Monitor oxygen saturation with a pulse oximeter
Get annual flu and pneumococcal vaccines
If breathlessness worsens, seek medical care

guidance: PAH is high blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries. Management: vasodilators (sildenafil, bosentan, prostacyclin analogs), diuretics, and oxygen. Treat underlying causes (connective tissue disease, congenital heart disease). Specialist care at tertiary centers. Free medications under government rare disease programs. Avoid pregnancy—high risk.
precautions: Do not get pregnant—pregnancy is extremely dangerous in PAH
Avoid strenuous exercise
Take vasodilators consistently—do not miss doses
Monitor for edema and weight gain
If syncope or severe breathlessness, seek emergency

symptoms: spider angiomas (spider-like blood vessels on skin)
guidance: Cirrhosis is the end stage of chronic liver injury. Management: treat the cause (stop alcohol, treat hepatitis B/C). Avoid hepatotoxic drugs. Low-sodium diet for ascites. Diuretics, lactulose for encephalopathy, and beta-blockers for varices. Variceal banding for bleeding. Liver transplant for eligible patients. Free care at government gastroenterology centers.
precautions: Absolute avoidance of alcohol
Use acetaminophen/paracetamol at minimal doses (do not exceed 2g/day)
Follow low-sodium diet (<2g/day)
Monitor for confusion—if present, use lactulose
Seek emergency care for vomiting blood or black stools

symptoms: in advanced: cirrhosis, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding
guidance: Complete abstinence from alcohol is the cornerstone. Nutritional support (high-protein, high-calorie), vitamins (especially thiamine, folate, B12). Corticosteroids for severe alcoholic hepatitis. Abstinence can reverse early damage and improve survival. Free de-addiction support and medical care at government hospitals.
precautions: Stop alcohol completely—no amount is safe
Take vitamin supplements (thiamine, folic acid)
Follow a high-protein, high-calorie diet
Monitor for bleeding and encephalopathy
If jaundice or ascites, seek medical care

symptoms: may present with acute or chronic hepatitis
guidance: Treatment: immunosuppressants—corticosteroids (prednisolone) and azathioprine are first-line. Lifelong therapy in most cases. Monitor liver function, transaminases, and immunoglobulin levels. In end-stage, liver transplant. Free immunosuppressants at government hospitals.
precautions: Take immunosuppressants regularly—do not stop without advice
Monitor for side effects (weight gain, osteoporosis, infections)
Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs
Annual liver function and ultrasound
If jaundice returns, seek care

symptoms: elevated alkaline phosphatase (ALP), positive AMA antibodies
guidance: PBC is a chronic cholestatic liver disease. Treatment: ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) improves liver biochemistry and delays progression. Obeticholic acid for non-responders. Manage pruritus with antihistamines, cholestyramine. Calcium and Vitamin D for bone health. Liver transplant for end-stage. Free UDCA at government hospitals.
precautions: Take UDCA regularly
Manage itching with prescribed medications
Calcium and Vitamin D supplementation
Annual liver function and ultrasound
If jaundice worsens, consult hepatologist

symptoms: often associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)
guidance: PSC is a progressive bile duct disease. No specific cure. UDCA may help liver biochemistry. ERCP for dominant strictures. Manage cholangitis with antibiotics. Liver transplant is the only cure for end-stage. Monitor for cholangiocarcinoma (annual imaging).
precautions: If you have IBD, get screened for PSC
Monitor for fever—may indicate cholangitis
Take UDCA as prescribed
Avoid alcohol
Regular imaging (MRI/MRCP) for strictures and cancer surveillance

symptoms: recurrent upper abdominal pain (biliary colic) after fatty meals
pain that may radiate to right shoulder
acute attacks with fever (if acute cholecystitis)
guidance: Chronic cholecystitis is usually due to gallstones. Management: low-fat diet, weight reduction. Elective cholecystectomy (laparoscopic) for symptomatic stones. Emergency surgery for acute cholecystitis. Free surgery at government hospitals under PMJAY. Asymptomatic stones can be observed.
precautions: Avoid high-fat, fried, and spicy foods
Maintain a healthy weight
If pain becomes severe or persistent, seek medical care
If fever and jaundice occur, urgent care needed
Post-cholecystectomy: eat small, frequent meals

symptoms: chronic abdominal pain (epigastric, radiating to back)
guidance: Management: pain management, pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with meals, low-fat diet, and diabetes management. Avoid alcohol completely. Smoking cessation. Endoscopic or surgical intervention for strictures or pseudocysts. Free enzyme supplementation at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid alcohol completely
Take pancreatic enzymes with every meal and snack
Follow a low-fat, high-protein diet
Monitor for diabetes—treat as needed
If pain is severe, seek medical care

symptoms: abdominal pain (often in right lower quadrant)
extraintestinal manifestations (joint pain, skin lesions, eye inflammation)
guidance: Crohn's is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease. Treatment: corticosteroids for acute flares, immunomodulators (azathioprine, methotrexate), biologics (anti-TNF agents like infliximab). Surgery for strictures or fistulas. Nutritional support (enteral feeding). Free biologics are available at government hospitals for eligible patients under NCD programs.
precautions: Take medications consistently—do not stop during remissions
Monitor for side effects of immunosuppressants (infections)
If diarrhea or abdominal pain worsens, seek care
Avoid NSAIDs (worsen IBD)
Get regular colonoscopy for cancer surveillance

guidance: UC is inflammation of the colon. Treatment: 5-aminosalicylates (mesalamine), corticosteroids for flares, immunomodulators, and biologics. Colectomy for severe or refractory cases. Free medications at government hospitals. Regular colonoscopy for cancer surveillance.
precautions: Take maintenance medications (mesalamine) daily to prevent flares
Avoid NSAIDs
If bloody diarrhea worsens, seek care
Monitor for toxic megacolon (severe abdominal distension, fever)
Regular colonoscopy after 8 years of disease

symptoms: chronic abdominal pain with altered bowel habits (diarrhea, constipation, or both)
no red flags (no weight loss, no blood, no nocturnal symptoms)
guidance: IBS is a functional bowel disorder. Management: diet (high-fiber, low-FODMAP), stress management, probiotics, and medications (antispasmodics, laxatives, antidiarrheals). CBT and hypnotherapy help. Rule out celiac and IBD. Free dietary counseling at government hospitals. Avoid triggers.
precautions: Keep a food diary to identify triggers (wheat, dairy, caffeine)
Reduce stress—yoga, meditation
Eat small, frequent meals
Avoid gas-producing foods (beans, cabbage, onions)
If symptoms persist or red flags appear, see a gastroenterologist

symptoms: may be associated with H. pylori infection or NSAID use
guidance: Chronic gastritis is inflammation of the gastric lining. Treatment: H. pylori eradication (triple therapy), avoid NSAIDs, and acid suppression (PPIs). Dietary: small frequent meals, avoid spicy and fried foods. Monitor for B12 deficiency (autoimmune gastritis). Free H. pylori testing and treatment at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid spicy, oily, and acidic foods
Do not take NSAIDs without medical advice
Take PPIs as prescribed (do not self-medicate long-term)
If black tarry stools or vomiting, seek care
If H. pylori positive, complete the full course

symptoms: burning epigastric pain (worse on empty stomach, relieved by food or antacids)
hematemesis (vomiting blood) or melena (black stools) if bleeding
guidance: Peptic ulcers are caused by H. pylori or NSAIDs. Treatment: H. pylori eradication, PPIs, and discontinue NSAIDs. Lifestyle: avoid spicy foods, alcohol, and smoking. Free treatment available. If bleeding or perforation, emergency surgery.
precautions: Complete H. pylori eradication course
Avoid NSAIDs, alcohol, and smoking
Take PPIs as prescribed
If black stools or coffee-ground vomiting, seek emergency care
Follow up for ulcer healing (endoscopy)

symptoms: regurgitation of food or sour liquid
worse after meals or lying down
guidance: GERD is chronic reflux. Management: lifestyle (weight loss, elevate head of bed, avoid large meals, avoid fatty/spicy foods), PPIs, and prokinetics. Complications: esophagitis, stricture, Barrett's esophagus (precancerous). Free endoscopy and medications at government hospitals. Long-term PPI use requires monitoring.
precautions: Avoid large meals and lying down immediately after eating
Elevate the head of your bed by 6-8 inches
Avoid spicy, fatty, and acidic foods
Do not smoke or consume alcohol
If dysphagia or weight loss, seek endoscopy

symptoms: joint pain that worsens with movement and weight-bearing
guidance: OA is the most common arthritis. Management: weight loss (reduces knee stress), low-impact exercise (walking, swimming, yoga), physiotherapy, and pain relief (paracetamol, topical NSAIDs). Oral NSAIDs short-term. Corticosteroid injections or hyaluronic acid for pain. Knee replacement for severe cases—free under PMJAY.
precautions: Maintain a healthy weight—every kg reduces knee load
Do regular low-impact exercises (walking, cycling)
Use a walking stick if needed to reduce joint stress
Avoid high-impact activities (running, jumping)
If severe pain or deformity, consult an orthopedic surgeon

symptoms: symmetrical joint pain and swelling (same joints on both sides)
joint deformity (swan neck, boutonnière) if untreated
affects small joints of hands and feet
guidance: RA is an autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. Early treatment with DMARDs (methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, sulfasalazine) prevents joint damage. Biologics (TNF inhibitors) for severe cases—available free at government hospitals under NCD programs. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Regular monitoring for complications (lung, eye, heart).
precautions: Start DMARDs early to prevent irreversible joint damage
Do not rely only on painkillers—need disease-modifying drugs
Monitor for infections while on immunosuppressants
Regular blood tests for liver function and blood counts
Physiotherapy to maintain joint function

symptoms: chronic low back pain and stiffness (worse in morning, improves with exercise)
inflammatory back pain (rest worsens, activity improves)
loss of spinal mobility, kyphosis (bent-forward posture)
guidance: AS is an inflammatory spondyloarthropathy. Treatment: NSAIDs (first-line), physiotherapy (spinal exercises), TNF inhibitors for severe cases—available free. Good posture, regular exercise (swimming, stretching). Genetic counseling for HLA-B27. Monitor for complications (cardiac, pulmonary).
precautions: Do daily spinal stretching and breathing exercises
Maintain good posture—sleep on a firm mattress
If NSAIDs insufficient, biologics are effective
Monitor for eye inflammation (uveitis)—seek care for red, painful eyes
Avoid smoking—can worsen lung involvement

symptoms: recurrent acute gout attacks (severe joint pain, swelling, redness—especially big toe)
tophi (hard, painless nodules under skin, especially on ears, elbows, fingers)
guidance: Gout is a disorder of uric acid metabolism. Chronic management: urate-lowering therapy (allopurinol, febuxostat) to keep uric acid <6 mg/dL. Lifestyle: avoid red meat, organ meats, shellfish, and alcohol (especially beer). Drink 2-3 liters of water daily. Colchicine or NSAIDs for acute flares. Free allopurinol at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid high-purine foods (red meat, organ meat, shellfish, anchovies)
Limit alcohol, especially beer
Drink plenty of water (2-3 L/day)
Take allopurinol consistently—do not stop, it prevents attacks
During acute attack, do not start allopurinol (wait until flare resolves)

symptoms: fractures with minimal trauma (hip, wrist, spine)
risk factors: early menopause, family history, thin body frame
guidance: Osteoporosis is a bone-thinning disease. Management: calcium (1000-1200 mg/day) and Vitamin D (800 IU/day) supplementation, weight-bearing exercise (walking, dancing). Bisphosphonates (alendronate) for high fracture risk—available free. DEXA scan for diagnosis and monitoring. Fall prevention is critical.
precautions: Take calcium and Vitamin D daily
Do weight-bearing exercises (walking, stair climbing)
Remove trip hazards at home to prevent falls (rugs, clutter)
Avoid alcohol and smoking
If on bisphosphonates, take with a glass of water on an empty stomach and stay upright for 30 min

guidance: SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease. Treatment: hydroxychloroquine (mainstay), corticosteroids for flares, and immunosuppressants (azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide) for organ-threatening disease (lupus nephritis, CNS involvement). Biologics (belimumab) for refractory cases—available free at tertiary centers. Avoid sun exposure, use sunscreen, and monitor for infections. Regular blood and urine monitoring.
precautions: Avoid sun exposure—use sunscreen (SPF 50+)
Do not stop hydroxychloroquine—it prevents flares
Monitor urine protein—if present, urgent nephrology referral
If fever, rash, or joint pain flares, seek care
Avoid live vaccines while on immunosuppressants

symptoms: Raynaud's phenomenon (fingers turn white/blue in cold)
guidance: Scleroderma is a rare autoimmune connective tissue disease. Management: vasodilators for Raynaud's, PPIs for GERD, immunosuppressants (methotrexate, mycophenolate) for skin and lung disease, and ACE inhibitors (captopril) for renal crisis—available free at government hospitals. Physical therapy, skin care, and regular monitoring of lung, kidney, and cardiac function.
precautions: Keep warm and avoid cold exposure to prevent Raynaud's
Take PPIs for GERD to prevent esophageal strictures
Monitor BP regularly—if sudden rise, seek care (renal crisis)
Do not smoke—worsens lung disease
Regular pulmonary function tests and echocardiograms

symptoms: can be primary or secondary to SLE/RA
guidance: Sjogren's is an autoimmune disorder affecting exocrine glands. Treatment: artificial tears, oral lubricants, pilocarpine to stimulate saliva, and hydroxychloroquine for systemic symptoms. Good dental hygiene to prevent caries. Monitor for lymphoma (parotid enlargement, weight loss). Free care at rheumatology clinics.
precautions: Use artificial tears frequently
Sip water frequently to relieve dry mouth
Maintain excellent dental hygiene (fluoride toothpaste)
Avoid medications that worsen dryness (antihistamines, tricyclic antidepressants)
If parotid enlargement or weight loss, seek specialist evaluation

symptoms: severe muscle pain and stiffness in shoulders, hips, and neck
difficulty getting up from a chair, raising arms
guidance: PMR is an inflammatory disorder. Treatment: low-dose corticosteroids (prednisolone) cause dramatic improvement—tapered slowly over months to years. Monitor for giant cell arteritis (GCA)—if headache, jaw claudication, or vision changes, urgent care. Free steroids at government hospitals. Bone protection (calcium, Vitamin D) during steroid therapy.
precautions: Do not stop prednisolone abruptly—taper only under medical guidance
Monitor for side effects: weight gain, diabetes, osteoporosis
If headache, vision loss, or jaw pain, seek emergency (GCA risk)
Take calcium and Vitamin D supplements
Regular ESR/CRP monitoring to guide treatment

symptoms: associated with psoriasis (scaly, red patches on skin)
guidance: Psoriatic arthritis is an inflammatory arthritis. Treatment: NSAIDs, DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine), and biologics (TNF inhibitors, IL-17 inhibitors) for moderate-severe disease—available free. Physiotherapy. Skin treatments for psoriasis. Regular monitoring for cardiovascular risk.
precautions: Treat both skin and joints—control of skin helps joint disease
Monitor for side effects of methotrexate (liver function, blood counts)
If you have psoriasis, screen for arthritis
Avoid smoking—worsens disease
Maintain a healthy weight to reduce joint stress

guidance: Hypothyroidism is a common condition, especially in women. Treatment: daily levothyroxine replacement—available free at government hospitals. Take on an empty stomach (30-60 minutes before breakfast). Monitor TSH every 6-12 months. Do not stop medication even if you feel well. Iodized salt prevents iodine deficiency hypothyroidism.
precautions: Take levothyroxine daily at the same time—do not skip
Do not take with iron, calcium, or antacids (separate by 4 hours)
If you become pregnant, the dose will increase—inform your doctor immediately
Monitor TSH regularly
Use iodized salt in cooking

symptoms: thickening of skin on shins (pretibial myxedema)
guidance: Graves' disease is an autoimmune hyperthyroidism. Treatment options: antithyroid drugs (methimazole, PTU), radioactive iodine therapy, or surgery (thyroidectomy). Antithyroid drugs are available free. Beta-blockers for symptom control. Monitor for agranulocytosis (fever, sore throat). Ophthalmopathy requires specialist care—smoking cessation is critical.
precautions: Take antithyroid medications consistently—do not stop abruptly
Report fever or sore throat immediately (risk of agranulocytosis)
Do not smoke—worsens eye disease
If pregnant, inform doctor (PTU is preferred in the first trimester)
Monitor thyroid function regularly

symptoms: xanthomas (fatty deposits on skin, eyelids, tendons)
elevated total cholesterol, LDL, or triglycerides
guidance: Dyslipidemia is a major risk factor for atherosclerosis. Management: lifestyle—heart-healthy diet (low saturated fat, trans fat, high fiber), regular exercise, weight loss. Statins are first-line drug therapy—available free at government NCD clinics. Monitor lipid profile every 6-12 months. Treat aggressively in high-risk patients (diabetes, CAD, hypertension).
precautions: Reduce saturated fats (red meat, butter, ghee, coconut oil)
Avoid trans fats (hydrogenated oils, commercially baked goods)
Eat more fiber (oats, fruits, vegetables, legumes)
Exercise regularly (30-45 min daily)
Do not stop statins without doctor's advice—even if cholesterol normalizes

symptoms: optic neuritis (painful vision loss in one eye)
Lhermitte's sign (electric shock sensation on neck flexion)
guidance: MS is an autoimmune demyelinating disease. Treatment: disease-modifying therapies (interferon, glatiramer, fingolimod, rituximab) to reduce relapses—available free at government hospitals. Acute relapses: high-dose corticosteroids. Multidisciplinary: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy. Avoid heat (worsens symptoms).
precautions: Take disease-modifying medications as prescribed
Avoid hot baths, saunas, and fever (heat exacerbates symptoms)
Exercise regularly but avoid overheating
Bladder training for urinary symptoms
Monitor for depression—seek mental health support

symptoms: resting tremor (pill-rolling, usually starts in one hand)
guidance: Parkinson's is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Treatment: levodopa/carbidopa (mainstay), dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors, and physiotherapy. Deep brain stimulation for advanced cases. Medications are free at government hospitals. Regular exercise (walking, tai chi, yoga) is proven to slow progression. Speech therapy for swallowing/dysarthria.
precautions: Take levodopa at consistent times—protein can interfere (take 1 hour before meals or 2 hours after)
Do not stop medication abruptly—can cause neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Exercise regularly—improves mobility
Fall prevention—remove trip hazards, use walking aids
If swallowing difficulty occurs, consult speech therapist and nutritionist

symptoms: memory loss that disrupts daily life (forgetting recent events, appointments)
difficulty with familiar tasks (cooking, managing finances)
confusion about time, place, or people
problems with language (finding words, following conversation)
guidance: Alzheimer's is the most common cause of dementia. Medications: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine) and memantine can slow progression—available free. Non-pharmacological: structured routines, memory aids, safety modifications, and caregiver support. Early diagnosis and planning. Free memory clinics at government hospitals.
precautions: Ensure home safety: lock away sharp objects, secure exits, install grab bars
Maintain a consistent daily routine
Do not argue with the person about false memories—redirect gently
Caregiver support groups are crucial to prevent burnout
If wandering is a risk, register with local police (tracking programs available)

symptoms: stepwise decline in cognition (sudden worsening after strokes)
guidance: Vascular dementia is caused by cerebrovascular disease. Treatment: control vascular risk factors (BP, diabetes, cholesterol), antiplatelet therapy (aspirin), and cognitive rehabilitation. Prevention is the best treatment. Free medications at NCD clinics. Supportive care and caregiver education.
precautions: Strictly control BP, blood sugar, and cholesterol
Take antiplatelet medications as prescribed
Maintain healthy diet and exercise
Fall prevention strategies
Monitor for new strokes (weakness, speech difficulty) and seek emergency care

symptoms: personality and behavior changes (apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy)
speech and language difficulty (fluent aphasia, word-finding problems)
relatively preserved memory in early stages
guidance: FTD is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder affecting the frontal and temporal lobes. No cure. Treatment: behavioral management, speech therapy, and medications for agitation (antipsychotics, SSRIs). Family support and caregiver education. Genetic counseling if familial.
precautions: Behavioral management strategies
Speech and occupational therapy
Address compulsive eating (monitor diet, lock food)
Caregiver support is essential
If aggression, discuss medications with psychiatrist

symptoms: REM sleep behavior disorder (acting out dreams)
guidance: DLB is a common type of dementia. Management: cholinesterase inhibitors may help hallucinations. Avoid antipsychotics (severe sensitivity). Treat Parkinsonism with levodopa cautiously (may worsen psychosis). Non-pharmacological: safety measures, routine, and caregiver support. Fall prevention.
precautions: Avoid typical antipsychotics—can be fatal
Use cholinesterase inhibitors as prescribed
Manage hallucinations—do not argue, use distraction
Fall prevention (gait and balance are impaired)
Monitor for orthostatic hypotension (dizziness on standing)

category: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS / Motor Neuron Disease)
symptoms: progressive muscle weakness (starts in limbs or bulbar)
no cognitive impairment in most cases
upper and lower motor neuron signs
guidance: ALS is a progressive neurodegenerative disease. Treatment: Riluzole and edaravone slow progression—available at government hospitals. Multidisciplinary care: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech therapy, and respiratory support. Nutritional support (high-calorie, PEG feeding if needed). Non-invasive ventilation for respiratory failure. Palliative care and advanced directives.
precautions: Riluzole should be taken consistently
Monitor weight and nutritional intake
If swallowing difficulty, consult speech therapist—aspiration is a major risk
Non-invasive ventilation (BiPAP) for respiratory symptoms
Plan for advanced care—discuss with family early

symptoms: fluctuating muscle weakness (worse with exertion, improves with rest)
guidance: MG is an autoimmune disease of the neuromuscular junction. Treatment: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine), immunosuppressants (corticosteroids, azathioprine), and thymectomy. Plasmapheresis and IVIG for crises. Free medications at government hospitals. Avoid medications that worsen MG (aminoglycosides, magnesium, beta-blockers).
precautions: Take pyridostigmine on time—do not skip doses
If muscle weakness worsens, seek care (myasthenic crisis risk)
Infections can trigger exacerbations—get prompt treatment
Avoid drugs that worsen MG (list provided by neurologist)
If difficulty breathing, go to emergency immediately

symptoms: types: generalized tonic-clonic (jerking, loss of consciousness), focal (partial, with or without impaired awareness), absence (brief staring spells)
guidance: Epilepsy is managed with antiepileptic drugs (AEDs)—available free at government hospitals. Monotherapy is preferred. Never miss doses. Regular monitoring of drug levels. Lifestyle: regular sleep, avoid alcohol, avoid triggering activities (swimming alone, driving). Most patients can live normal lives with treatment.
precautions: Never miss AED doses—this can trigger breakthrough seizures
Maintain a regular sleep schedule—sleep deprivation triggers seizures
Do not drive until seizure-free for at least 1 year
During a seizure: protect from injury, do not put anything in mouth, time the seizure
If seizure lasts >5 minutes, call 108 (status epilepticus)

symptoms: headache occurring ≥15 days per month, for ≥3 months
at least 8 days with migraine features (unilateral, pulsatile, moderate-severe, nausea, photophobia, phonophobia)
neurological: visual changes, weakness, or speech difficulty (aura)
guidance: Chronic migraine management: lifestyle (regular sleep, meals, hydration, avoid triggers), acute medications (triptans, NSAIDs) limited to ≤2 days/week to prevent medication-overuse headache, and preventive medications (propranolol, amitriptyline, topiramate, flunarizine). Botox and CGRP monoclonal antibodies are available at specialized centers. Free preventive medications at government hospitals.
precautions: Identify and avoid triggers (stress, certain foods, sleep changes)
Do not overuse acute pain medications (>2 days/week) to avoid rebound headaches
Take preventive medications consistently
Stay well-hydrated
If aura occurs with new weakness, seek emergency (rule out stroke)

symptoms: not aggravated by routine physical activity
may have photophobia or phonophobia (but not both)
stress and muscle tension are triggers
guidance: Treatment: acute—simple analgesics (paracetamol, NSAIDs) but limit to ≤2 days/week. Preventive: tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), stress management, relaxation therapy, CBT, and physiotherapy (neck muscle relaxation). Free counseling at government hospitals. Good sleep hygiene.
precautions: Limit analgesic use to avoid medication-overuse headache
Practice stress management (yoga, deep breathing)
Improve posture (ergonomic work setup)
Regular exercise
If headache pattern changes, see a neurologist

symptoms: severe, strictly unilateral pain (orbital, supraorbital, or temporal)
frequency: once every other day to 8 times per day
associated with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms (red/watery eye, nasal congestion, ptosis, miosis)
guidance: Cluster headache is the most painful headache. Acute treatment: high-flow oxygen, subcutaneous sumatriptan, or intranasal triptans. Preventive: verapamil (high dose, with ECG monitoring), lithium, corticosteroids (short-term). Neurologist referral is essential. Oxygen is available at some government hospitals. Avoid alcohol and smoking during cluster periods.
precautions: Do not take triptans if you have coronary artery disease
If on verapamil, monitor ECG and heart rate
Avoid alcohol during cluster periods (triggers attacks)
Oxygen therapy is safe and effective if available
If new headache, do not self-diagnose—see a neurologist

symptoms: sudden, severe, sharp, stabbing, electric shock-like pain in the distribution of one or more branches of the trigeminal nerve (face, jaw, eye)
triggered by trivial stimuli (talking, chewing, brushing teeth, cold air)
guidance: First-line treatment: carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine—available free at government hospitals. If refractory, gabapentin, baclofen, or lamotrigine. Surgical options (microvascular decompression, radiofrequency, gamma knife) for refractory cases. Neurologist/neurosurgeon consultation.
precautions: Take carbamazepine regularly—do not stop abruptly (can cause seizures)
Monitor for side effects (dizziness, hyponatremia, rash)
Avoid triggers if possible (cold wind, hard foods)
If skin rash (Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk), stop medication immediately and seek care
Dental examination to rule out dental causes

symptoms: tender points (pressure points on neck, shoulders, back, hips)
headaches, irritable bowel syndrome, depression, anxiety
guidance: Fibromyalgia is a chronic pain syndrome. Management: patient education, graded exercise (walking, swimming), CBT, and stress management. Medications: pregabalin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, and gabapentin—available free at government hospitals. Treat comorbidities (depression, IBS). Support groups. Avoid opioids (generally not effective).
precautions: Exercise regularly (start slow and increase gradually)
Maintain a regular sleep schedule
Manage stress (yoga, meditation)
Do not rely on opioids for pain—they are not effective for fibromyalgia
If depression is present, treat with antidepressants

symptoms: worsened by physical or mental exertion (post-exertional malaise)
headaches, sore throat, tender lymph nodes
guidance: CFS is a complex disorder. Management: pacing (balance activity and rest), CBT, graded exercise therapy (carefully monitored). Address sleep disturbances and depression. Free counseling at government hospitals. Avoid extreme exertion. Support groups.
precautions: Pacing is key—do not push through fatigue (worsens symptoms)
Maintain a regular sleep schedule
Eat balanced meals
If mood is low, seek mental health support
Avoid overexertion leading to post-exertional malaise

symptoms: signs of underlying chronic disease (infection, inflammation, malignancy)
low serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin
guidance: ACD is secondary to chronic inflammatory conditions (RA, SLE, CKD, infection, cancer). Treatment: treat the underlying condition. Erythropoietin for CKD-associated anemia. Iron supplementation is not effective (iron is trapped). Managing the primary disease improves anemia. Free care for underlying conditions at government hospitals.
precautions: Do not take iron supplements without a doctor's advice—they are ineffective in ACD
Treat the underlying chronic disease
Monitor hemoglobin regularly
If anemia worsens, investigate for other causes (B12, folate, bleeding)
Erythropoietin if indicated (CKD)

symptoms: sickle cell crises (severe pain in bones, chest, abdomen)
hand-foot syndrome (dactylitis in children, less in adults)
acute chest syndrome (chest pain, fever, respiratory distress)
chronic complications: avascular necrosis, leg ulcers, retinopathy
guidance: Sickle cell disease is a genetic hemoglobinopathy. Management: hydroxyurea reduces crises—available free. Pain management, hydration, and prompt treatment of infections. Penicillin prophylaxis (up to age 5 or lifelong if splenectomized). Pneumococcal and meningococcal vaccines. Blood transfusions for severe anemia or stroke prevention. Genetic counseling.
precautions: Stay well-hydrated—dehydration triggers crises
Avoid extreme cold
Take hydroxyurea consistently—it reduces crisis frequency
Seek care for any fever or pain crisis promptly
If chest pain or respiratory distress, seek emergency (acute chest syndrome)

symptoms: iron overload (due to repeated transfusions): cardiac, hepatic, endocrine dysfunction
guidance: Thalassemia major requires lifelong regular blood transfusions (every 2-4 weeks) and iron chelation therapy (deferasirox, deferoxamine) to prevent iron overload—available free at government hospitals. Bone marrow transplant is the only cure. Prevention: carrier screening and prenatal diagnosis. Endocrine monitoring for diabetes, hypothyroidism, and osteoporosis.
precautions: Adhere to regular transfusion schedule
Take iron chelation therapy consistently—iron overload is the leading cause of death
Monitor cardiac function (echocardiogram, MRI) annually
Avoid iron-containing supplements (already iron overloaded)
If splenectomy is done, take lifelong antibiotics for infection prevention

symptoms: spontaneous bleeding into joints (hemarthrosis) causing pain, swelling, and deformity
prolonged bleeding after trauma or surgery
guidance: Hemophilia A is an X-linked bleeding disorder. Treatment: factor VIII replacement (prophylactic or on-demand)—available free under government rare disease programs. Avoid intramuscular injections, aspirin, NSAIDs. Dental care with factor cover. Genetic counseling. Joint physiotherapy for chronic hemarthropathy.
precautions: Avoid contact sports and activities with high injury risk
Do not take aspirin or NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen)—use paracetamol for pain
If you have a bleed, factor replacement is urgent
If head injury, seek emergency care immediately even if no symptoms
Wear medical alert ID

symptoms: same as Hemophilia A (joint bleeds, muscle bleeds, easy bruising)
guidance: Treatment: factor IX replacement—available free under government rare disease programs. Prophylaxis or on-demand. Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs. Genetic counseling. Joint physiotherapy. Free factor concentrates at designated centers.
precautions: Same as Hemophilia A: avoid NSAIDs, contact sports, and head injuries
Factor IX replacement is life-saving
Carry a medical alert ID
If joint swelling, early factor infusion prevents permanent damage
Dental procedures require factor cover

symptoms: prolonged bleeding from cuts and gums
prolonged bleeding after surgery or dental work
guidance: vWD is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Treatment: desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild cases; factor concentrate for severe. Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid) for mucosal bleeding. Avoid aspirin. Free desmopressin at government hospitals. Gynecological consultation for heavy periods.
precautions: Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs
If heavy periods, consult a gynecologist—may need hormonal therapy
Inform dentists and surgeons about the condition
If bleeding, apply pressure and seek care
Desmopressin is effective but monitor for hyponatremia

symptoms: leg heaviness, aching, fatigue (worse at end of day, relieved by elevation)
skin changes: stasis dermatitis (brown discoloration, itching, scaling)
guidance: CVI is caused by damaged valves in leg veins. Management: compression stockings (graduated, 20-30 mmHg), leg elevation, exercise (walking), and weight loss. Avoid prolonged standing. For ulcers: wound care, compression. Sclerotherapy or surgery for varicose veins. Free compression stockings at government hospitals.
precautions: Wear compression stockings during the day (remove at night)
Elevate legs above heart level for 15-20 minutes several times a day
Avoid prolonged sitting or standing
If leg ulcers, keep clean and seek wound care
If swelling suddenly increases, rule out DVT

symptoms: dilated, tortuous, superficial veins in legs
guidance: Varicose veins are a cosmetic and functional problem. Management: compression stockings, leg elevation, exercise, and weight loss. Sclerotherapy, endovenous ablation, or surgery for symptomatic or cosmetic concerns. Free surgical care at government hospitals.
precautions: Wear compression stockings
Elevate legs when resting
Avoid prolonged standing
Regular walking
If pain, redness, or swelling, rule out superficial thrombophlebitis

symptoms: numbness, tingling, burning pain in hands and feet (stocking-glove distribution)
loss of sensation (danger: cannot feel wounds)
guidance: Neuropathy is a common complication of diabetes. Prevention: strict glycemic control. Treatment: pain management with gabapentin, pregabalin, or duloxetine—available free at government hospitals. Foot care: daily inspection, moisturize, wear proper shoes, do not walk barefoot. Regular podiatry evaluation.
precautions: Check feet daily for cuts, blisters, or sores—use a mirror if needed
Do not walk barefoot
Wear well-fitting, soft shoes
Moisturize feet (but not between toes)
If a foot ulcer develops, seek medical care immediately (delays lead to amputation)

symptoms: sudden vision loss (vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment)
guidance: Diabetic retinopathy is the leading cause of blindness in working-age adults. Screening: annual fundoscopy for all diabetics. Treatment: strict glycemic and BP control. For proliferative or macular edema: laser photocoagulation and anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept)—available free at government hospitals. Early detection prevents blindness.
precautions: Get an annual dilated eye exam (fundoscopy)
Control blood sugar and BP
If sudden vision loss or floaters, seek emergency ophthalmology care
Do not ignore vision changes
If pregnant with diabetes, more frequent eye exams are needed

symptoms: early: microalbuminuria (detected on urine test, no symptoms)
guidance: Diabetic nephropathy is the leading cause of CKD in India. Management: strict glycemic control, BP control with ACE inhibitors or ARBs (renoprotective), low-salt diet, and protein restriction. Monitor urine microalbumin annually. Free ACE inhibitors and ARBs at government hospitals. Dialysis for end-stage—free under PMNDP.
precautions: Get urine microalbumin test annually
Take ACE inhibitors/ARBs as prescribed (even if BP is normal—they protect kidneys)
Limit salt and protein intake as advised
Control blood sugar and BP
If swelling or foamy urine, seek care

symptoms: non-healing sore or ulcer on the foot
pain (may be absent due to neuropathy)
guidance: Foot ulcers are a major cause of amputation. Treatment: wound debridement, offloading (special shoes/cast), infection control (antibiotics), and revascularization if PAD. Glycemic control. Multidisciplinary: diabetologist, podiatrist, vascular surgeon. Free wound care and antibiotics at government hospitals. Prevention is key—daily foot inspection.
precautions: Daily foot inspection (use a mirror)
Do not walk barefoot
Wear diabetic shoes (wide-toed)
See a doctor immediately for any non-healing wound
If gangrene or fever, seek emergency care

symptoms: often asymptomatic in early stages (silent thief of sight)
gradual loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision)
family history is a risk factor
guidance: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. Screening: annual eye exam with tonometry and fundoscopy for all >40 years, especially with family history. Treatment: topical eye drops (prostaglandins, beta-blockers, carbonic anhydrase inhibitors)—available free at government hospitals. Laser trabeculoplasty or surgery if needed. Early detection prevents blindness.
precautions: Get regular eye checkups (especially if family history)
Use eye drops consistently—do not skip doses
If you experience eye pain, redness, or sudden vision loss, seek emergency (acute angle-closure glaucoma)
Follow up with ophthalmologist for IOP monitoring
Do not stop drops without consulting

symptoms: glare (difficulty with bright lights, night driving)
guidance: Cataract is the most common cause of blindness in India. Treatment: surgical removal with intraocular lens implantation—available free under the National Blindness Control Programme at government hospitals. Surgery is safe and highly effective. Do not delay—cataract surgery restores vision.
precautions: Get annual eye exams
If vision is affecting daily activities, consider surgery—do not wait until 'ripe'
Post-surgery: use prescribed eye drops, avoid rubbing the eye
Avoid heavy lifting for 2 weeks after surgery
Wear sunglasses to reduce glare

symptoms: central vision loss (blurry or distorted area in the center of vision)
guidance: AMD affects the macula (central retina). Dry AMD: no specific treatment; supplements (AREDS2: vitamins C, E, zinc, lutein, zeaxanthin) may slow progression. Wet AMD: anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, aflibercept)—available free at government hospitals. Early detection via Amsler grid home testing.
precautions: Monitor vision with Amsler grid daily
If you notice sudden changes, see an ophthalmologist immediately
Take AREDS2 supplements if recommended
Do not smoke—smoking worsens AMD
Protect eyes from UV light (sunglasses)

symptoms: progressive loss of peripheral vision (tunnel vision)
loss of central vision in advanced stages
guidance: RP is a genetic retinal degeneration. No cure. Management: genetic counseling, low-vision aids, orientation and mobility training. Vitamin A palmitate (moderate dose) may slow progression in some—consult ophthalmologist. Free low-vision rehabilitation at government hospitals. Avoid driving at night.
precautions: Genetic counseling for family
Use low-vision aids (magnifiers, mobility canes)
Do not smoke
If taking Vitamin A, do not exceed dose (can be hepatotoxic)
Regular ophthalmology follow-up

symptoms: gradual hearing loss, especially high frequencies (difficulty hearing women's/children's voices)
difficulty understanding speech in noisy environments
no history of ear infections or ear pain
guidance: Age-related hearing loss is common. Management: hearing aids (available free or subsidized at government hospitals), assistive listening devices, and communication strategies. Avoid loud noise exposure. If sudden hearing loss, seek emergency (may be treatable with steroids).
precautions: Use hearing aids as prescribed
Avoid loud noises (wear ear protection)
Inform family/friends to speak clearly and face you
If sudden hearing loss, seek emergency ENT care
Regular hearing assessments

symptoms: perception of ringing, buzzing, hissing, or roaring sound in the ears without external source
may be associated with hearing loss
can cause distress, anxiety, and sleep disturbance
guidance: Tinnitus is a symptom, not a disease. Management: treat underlying cause (hearing loss, cerumen, vascular, TMJ). Sound therapy (masking devices), CBT, and tinnitus retraining therapy. Avoid silence. Reduce stress. Free counseling at government ENT clinics. Rule out serious causes (acoustic neuroma).
precautions: Use background noise (white noise, fans) to mask tinnitus
Reduce stress and anxiety—CBT helps
Avoid loud noise exposure
If tinnitus is unilateral and pulsatile, see an ENT
Do not use over-the-counter 'tinnitus cures' without evidence

symptoms: dribbling at the end of urination
guidance: BPH is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate. Management: alpha-blockers (tamsulosin) and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride)—available free at government hospitals. Lifestyle: reduce caffeine/alcohol, double voiding, and timed voiding. Surgery (TURP) for severe symptoms or complications. Free surgery at government hospitals.
precautions: Limit fluids before bedtime to reduce nocturia
Avoid caffeine and alcohol—they irritate the bladder
Do not take decongestants (can worsen symptoms)
If you cannot urinate, seek emergency care (acute urinary retention)
Monitor for blood in urine—rule out prostate cancer

symptoms: difficulty achieving or maintaining an erection sufficient for sexual intercourse
may be associated with vascular disease, diabetes, or psychological factors
guidance: Erectile dysfunction is often a vascular problem. Management: lifestyle (exercise, weight loss, smoking cessation, diabetes/BP control). PDE5 inhibitors (sildenafil, tadalafil)—available free at government hospitals (may require prescription). Psychotherapy for psychological causes. Treat underlying conditions.
precautions: Do not take PDE5 inhibitors with nitrates (risk of severe hypotension)
If you have heart disease, consult cardiologist before taking
Lifestyle changes may improve ED without medication
If sudden loss of erection, rule out cardiovascular disease
Counseling if anxiety is the cause

symptoms: pelvic or perineal pain (lower abdomen, testicles, penis, between scrotum and anus)
may be chronic, waxing and waning
guidance: Chronic pelvic pain syndrome. Management: alpha-blockers, anti-inflammatory drugs, pelvic floor physiotherapy, and stress management. Antibiotics are not effective (unless infection proven). Free medications at government hospitals. Avoid triggers (spicy foods, prolonged sitting).
precautions: Avoid prolonged sitting—take breaks
Reduce spicy foods, caffeine, and alcohol
Pelvic floor physiotherapy
Warm baths may relieve pain
If acute symptoms (fever, chills), seek care (may be acute prostatitis)

symptoms: may be asymptomatic with high residual urine volume (>300 ml)
guidance: Chronic retention can be due to BPH, neurological disease, or bladder dysfunction. Management: treat the cause (alpha-blockers for BPH, intermittent self-catheterization, surgery). Monitor renal function. Free urology care at government hospitals. Avoid bladder stones and UTIs.
precautions: Do not ignore difficulty urinating—can damage kidneys
If you have a neurogenic bladder, intermittent catheterization is important
Monitor for UTIs
Avoid caffeine and alcohol
If acute retention (cannot urinate), emergency Foley catheterization needed

symptoms: urinary urgency (sudden urge to urinate that is difficult to defer)
guidance: OAB is common. Management: behavioral therapy (bladder training, pelvic floor exercises, fluid management), and anticholinergics or beta-3 agonists (mirabegron). Free medications at government hospitals. Rule out UTI. If severe, Botox or neuromodulation.
precautions: Bladder training: delay voiding gradually
Pelvic floor exercises (Kegels)
Limit caffeine, alcohol, and citrus (irritants)
Double void (urinate, wait, urinate again)
If urgency with fever or pain, rule out infection

symptoms: wheals (raised, itchy, red or skin-colored welts) lasting <24 hours
associated with angioedema (swelling of lips, eyelids, hands, feet, genitals) in 40%
itching can be severe, affecting sleep and daily activities
guidance: Chronic urticaria is often autoimmune. Management: non-sedating antihistamines (second-generation) at higher doses—available free. If refractory, add montelukast, omalizumab (anti-IgE—available at some government hospitals). Avoid triggers (NSAIDs, alcohol, stress). Refer to dermatologist.
precautions: Take antihistamines daily—do not skip
Avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (can worsen)
Avoid alcohol and hot environments
If angioedema with breathing difficulty, seek emergency
Stress management—stress can trigger flares

symptoms: well-demarcated, red, scaly plaques covered with silvery-white scales
most commonly on elbows, knees, scalp, and lower back
guidance: Psoriasis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease. Treatment: topical corticosteroids, vitamin D analogs (calcipotriol), and phototherapy (UVB/PUVA)—available free at government hospitals. Systemic: methotrexate, cyclosporine, and biologics (TNF, IL-17, IL-23 inhibitors) for severe disease. Avoid triggers (stress, infections, alcohol).
precautions: Use topical treatments consistently
Avoid picking scales (can cause Koebner phenomenon)
If on methotrexate, monitor liver function and blood counts
Do not smoke—worsens psoriasis
If joint pain occurs, see a rheumatologist (psoriatic arthritis)

symptoms: hair in affected areas may turn white (leukotrichia)
guidance: Vitiligo is an autoimmune depigmentation. Treatment: topical corticosteroids, calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus), and phototherapy (narrowband UVB). In stable cases, surgical transplantation. Sun protection is crucial (depigmented skin burns easily). Free phototherapy at government dermatology centers. Camouflage cosmetics.
precautions: Use broad-spectrum sunscreen (SPF 50+) on depigmented areas
Avoid sunburn—white patches burn easily
If on phototherapy, follow schedule strictly
Psychological support if distressing
Do not use quack remedies—can cause scarring

symptoms: sudden, patchy hair loss (well-demarcated round/oval bald patches)
may involve scalp, beard, eyebrows, eyelashes
exclamation mark hairs at the periphery
may progress to alopecia totalis (all scalp) or universalis (whole body)
nails may have pitting or ridging
guidance: Alopecia areata is autoimmune. Treatment: topical corticosteroids, intralesional steroids, and minoxidil. In severe cases, systemic corticosteroids, DPCP, or JAK inhibitors (available at some centers). Free treatment at government hospitals. Psychological support. Spontaneous regrowth is possible.
precautions: Do not panic—spontaneous regrowth occurs in many
Avoid stress (may trigger exacerbations)
If on systemic steroids, monitor side effects
Wear wigs or head coverings if desired
Consult a dermatologist for treatment options

symptoms: recurrent, painful, inflamed nodules, abscesses, and sinus tracts in apocrine gland-bearing areas (axillae, groin, perineum, inframammary)
often associated with obesity and smoking
guidance: HS is a chronic inflammatory skin disease. Management: weight loss, smoking cessation, topical clindamycin, oral antibiotics (doxycycline, rifampicin), and biologics (adalimumab—available at some centers). Surgery for refractory sinus tracts. Free care at government dermatology clinics.
precautions: Lose weight—significant improvement
Stop smoking—worsens disease
Wear loose-fitting clothes
Avoid shaving affected areas (can trigger)
Warm compresses for painful nodules

symptoms: pruritic, polygonal, flat-topped, violaceous papules and plaques
often on wrists, ankles, lower back
oral lichen planus: white reticular patches (Wickham's striae) in the mouth
Koebner phenomenon (new lesions at sites of trauma)
guidance: Lichen planus is an inflammatory skin disease. Treatment: topical corticosteroids, oral antihistamines, and for oral involvement, topical corticosteroids (clobetasol gel). Severe cases: systemic corticosteroids or phototherapy. Free treatment at government hospitals. Monitor oral lesions for malignancy (rare).
precautions: Use topical steroids as prescribed
Avoid scratching—can cause Koebnerization
For oral lesions, avoid spicy and acidic foods
If oral lesions persist, regular dental/ENT follow-up
Stress management

symptoms: chronic pain in the lower back (lumbar region)
worse with sitting or standing, relieved by lying down
may radiate to buttocks and thighs
associated with degenerative changes (osteophytes, disc degeneration)
guidance: Management: exercise (core strengthening, stretching), physiotherapy, weight loss, and pain relief (paracetamol, NSAIDs short-term). Maintain good posture and ergonomic support. Avoid bed rest—stay active. For radiculopathy (sciatica), imaging and specialist care. Free physiotherapy at government hospitals. Surgery for severe cases.
precautions: Stay active—bed rest worsens back pain
Strengthen core muscles
Maintain proper posture (sit up straight, use lumbar support)
Lift heavy objects correctly (bend knees, not back)
If leg weakness or bowel/bladder dysfunction, seek emergency (cauda equina)

symptoms: pain radiating to shoulders and arms
numbness or tingling in arms and hands
spurling test positive (pain on neck extension and rotation)
guidance: Management: physiotherapy (range of motion, strengthening), pain relief (paracetamol, topical NSAIDs), cervical collar (short-term), and posture correction (ergonomic workstations). If radiculopathy, imaging (MRI). Free physiotherapy at government hospitals. Surgery for cervical myelopathy.
precautions: Maintain good posture—avoid forward head position (computer, phone)
Use an ergonomic chair
Neck strengthening exercises
Avoid heavy lifting
If weakness or gait disturbance, see a neurosurgeon (myelopathy)

symptoms: may have acute exacerbations (disc herniation with radiculopathy)
guidance: Management: physiotherapy, core strengthening, weight management, pain relief, and lifestyle modifications. Avoid smoking (decreases disc nutrition). For herniation with neurological symptoms, imaging and specialist intervention. Free physiotherapy at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid prolonged sitting—take breaks
Strengthen back and core muscles
Lift with your legs
If severe leg pain or weakness, see a specialist
Smoking accelerates disc degeneration—stop

symptoms: frequent bone fractures with minimal trauma
guidance: OI is a genetic disorder of collagen. Management: bisphosphonates (pamidronate) to reduce fractures—available free at government hospitals under rare disease programs. Physical therapy to improve mobility and muscle strength. Fall prevention. Genetic counseling. Dental care. Hearing aids if needed.
precautions: Fall prevention is critical
Avoid contact sports
Take bisphosphonates as prescribed
If you have OI, regular dental and ENT care
Genetic counseling for family planning

guidance: EDS is a connective tissue disorder. Management: physiotherapy (joint protection, muscle strengthening), pain management (paracetamol, avoid NSAIDs if GI issues), and occupational therapy. Avoid contact sports. POTS management: hydration, salt, and compression stockings. Genetic counseling.
precautions: Protect joints—avoid hyperextension
Strengthen muscles around joints
Avoid high-impact activities
If skin wounds, sutures may need to stay longer
Monitor for aortic dilation (echocardiogram)

symptoms: tall stature, long limbs (arm span > height)
guidance: Marfan is a genetic connective tissue disorder. Management: cardiology follow-up with echocardiograms (monitor aortic root), beta-blockers or ARBs to slow aortic dilation, and prophylactic surgery when aortic diameter reaches threshold. Avoid strenuous exercise and contact sports. Genetic counseling. Free cardiology care at government hospitals.
precautions: Avoid strenuous exercise and competitive sports
Regular echocardiograms (every 6-12 months)
Take beta-blockers/ARBs as prescribed
If sudden chest pain or back pain, seek emergency (aortic dissection)
Ophthalmology follow-up for lens dislocation and glaucoma

symptoms: itching (pruritus), especially after a hot shower (aquagenic pruritus)
high risk of thrombosis (stroke, DVT, MI)
guidance: PV is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Management: phlebotomy (to keep hematocrit <45%), aspirin (low dose) to reduce thrombosis risk, and cytoreduction (hydroxyurea) for high-risk patients. Free phlebotomy and hydroxyurea at government hospitals. Monitor for progression to myelofibrosis or AML.
precautions: Adhere to phlebotomy schedule
Take aspirin as prescribed (unless contraindicated)
If you experience sudden headache, vision changes, or weakness, seek emergency (thrombosis)
Stay well-hydrated
Monitor blood counts regularly

symptoms: risk of thrombosis (stroke, DVT) and bleeding
guidance: ET is a myeloproliferative neoplasm. Management: low-dose aspirin for all patients. Cytoreduction (hydroxyurea, anagrelide) for high-risk (age >60, history of thrombosis). Free medications at government hospitals. Monitor for progression.
precautions: Take aspirin as prescribed
Monitor platelet counts regularly
If sudden severe headache or weakness, seek emergency (stroke)
Avoid smoking—increases thrombosis risk
If bleeding (epistaxis, gums), inform doctor

guidance: Myelofibrosis is a myeloproliferative neoplasm with bone marrow fibrosis. Management: supportive care (transfusions for anemia), JAK2 inhibitors (ruxolitinib)—available free at government tertiary centers, and stem cell transplant (curative). Splenectomy for massive splenomegaly if refractory. Monitor for transformation to AML.
precautions: Take JAK2 inhibitors as prescribed
Monitor for infections (immunosuppression)
If severe abdominal pain (splenic infarction), seek care
If fever, seek care promptly
Genetic counseling (JAK2 V617F mutation testing)

symptoms: usually in chronic phase at diagnosis
guidance: CML is caused by the Philadelphia chromosome (BCR-ABL). Treatment: tyrosine kinase inhibitors (imatinib) are highly effective and available free at government hospitals. Regular monitoring with PCR for BCR-ABL (quantitative). Allogeneic stem cell transplant for refractory or accelerated phase. Good long-term survival with imatinib.
precautions: Take imatinib consistently at the same time each day with food
Monitor blood counts regularly (CBC, differential)
If you develop rash, diarrhea, or edema, inform doctor (side effects)
Do not stop medication without consulting—can cause relapse
If you develop bone pain or fever, seek care (blast crisis risk)

guidance: MDS is a clonal bone marrow disorder. Management: supportive care (transfusions, growth factors), hypomethylating agents (azacitidine) for high-risk—available free at government hospitals. Allogeneic stem cell transplant is curative. Genetic testing for cytogenetic abnormalities.
precautions: Monitor for infections—prompt treatment
If transfusion-dependent, monitor iron overload and use chelation
If high-risk, discuss transplant options early
Regular blood counts and bone marrow assessments
Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic drugs

guidance: CLL is a mature B-cell neoplasm. Management: watchful waiting in early stages. Treatment: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib), fludarabine, or venetoclax—available free at government tertiary centers. Monitor for infections (hypogammaglobulinemia). Regular blood counts and physical exams.
precautions: Watch for signs of infection—prompt treatment
If you develop fever, night sweats, or lymph node swelling, inform doctor
Avoid live vaccines
If on ibrutinib, monitor for atrial fibrillation and bleeding
Good hand hygiene and avoid sick contacts

symptoms: bone pain (often back, ribs, skull—lytic lesions)
guidance: Multiple myeloma is a plasma cell neoplasm. Treatment: proteasome inhibitors (bortezomib), immunomodulators (lenalidomide), corticosteroids, and autologous stem cell transplant—available free at government hospitals under rare disease programs. Bisphosphonates for bone lesions. Monitor renal function and calcium.
precautions: Hydrate well to prevent renal failure
If bone pain, avoid heavy lifting—risk of fracture
Monitor for infections—prompt treatment
If you have hypercalcemia symptoms (nausea, confusion), seek care
Consider novel agents (carfilzomib, daratumumab) at specialized centers

symptoms: progressive, symmetric muscle weakness (proximal and distal)
numbness, tingling in hands and feet
guidance: CIDP is an immune-mediated neuropathy. Treatment: IVIG, corticosteroids (prednisolone), or plasmapheresis—available free at government hospitals. Response is often good. Physiotherapy and occupational therapy. Long-term maintenance therapy needed. Free IVIG at designated centers.
precautions: Take corticosteroids/immunosuppressants as prescribed—do not stop abruptly
Monitor for side effects (weight gain, high BP, diabetes)
Physiotherapy is essential for maintaining mobility
If difficulty breathing or swallowing, seek emergency
Regular neurology follow-up

guidance: AIHA is an autoimmune disorder. Management: corticosteroids (prednisolone) are first-line—available free. Rituximab for refractory cases. Splenectomy for chronic disease. Folate supplementation. Avoid infections (can trigger hemolysis). Monitor hemoglobin and hemolysis markers.
precautions: Take steroids as prescribed—taper slowly under medical supervision
Avoid infections—prompt treatment
If jaundice or dark urine worsens, seek care
Folate supplements are important
Monitor for side effects of long-term steroids

symptoms: pain in response to normally non-painful stimuli (allodynia)
guidance: Management: multidisciplinary—pain education, CBT, graded exercise, and medications (antidepressants, anticonvulsants—pregabalin, gabapentin). Avoid opioids (ineffective and harmful). Free physiotherapy and counseling at government hospitals. Pain clinics in tertiary centers.
precautions: Do not rely on opioids—they worsen pain in the long term
Graded exercise is beneficial
CBT helps coping
Treat depression/anxiety if present
Set realistic goals

symptoms: persistent neck pain after a whiplash injury (motor vehicle accident)
guidance: Management: physiotherapy (neck exercises, posture correction), pain relief (paracetamol, NSAIDs short-term), and reassurance. Avoid neck collars (can cause deconditioning). Free physiotherapy at government hospitals. Psychological support if chronic.
precautions: Stay active—do not use collars long-term
Neck strengthening exercises
Ergonomic adjustments
If weakness or numbness, see a specialist
Manage stress

symptoms: facial pain or pressure (over cheeks, forehead, eyes)
guidance: Chronic sinusitis is inflammation of the sinuses lasting >12 weeks. Management: nasal saline irrigation, intranasal corticosteroids, and antibiotics for acute exacerbations. In refractory cases, surgery (FESS) for anatomical obstruction. Free ENT care at government hospitals.
precautions: Nasal saline irrigation daily
Use intranasal corticosteroids consistently
Avoid smoking and air pollution
If you have asthma or allergies, manage them
If vision changes or severe headache, seek emergency (orbital complication)

symptoms: popping, clicking, or grating sounds in the jaw joint
locking of the jaw (open or closed)
guidance: TMJ disorders are often self-limiting. Management: soft diet, avoid chewing gum, jaw exercises (stretching, relaxing), heat/cold packs, NSAIDs for pain, and stress management. If persistent, dental splint. Free dental care at government hospitals. Referral to oral/maxillofacial surgeon if severe.
precautions: Avoid hard or chewy foods
Apply warm compresses
Practice stress reduction (massage, relaxation)
Do not chew gum
If jaw locks, see a dentist or ENT

symptoms: burning sensation in the mouth, especially with spicy food
blanching, pale mucosa with fibrous bands
guidance: Oral submucous fibrosis is strongly associated with areca nut (pan, gutkha) chewing. Treatment: cessation of areca nut and tobacco. Physiotherapy for trismus (jaw opening exercises), steroids, and antioxidants. Surgical release for severe cases. Regular follow-up for malignant transformation. Free government dental/ENT care.
precautions: Stop chewing areca nut, pan, gutkha, and tobacco completely
Practice jaw-stretching exercises
Avoid spicy foods
Regular oral cancer screening
If ulcer or growth, seek immediate biopsy

symptoms: white patches or plaques in the mouth that cannot be scraped off
most common on buccal mucosa, tongue, floor of mouth
guidance: Leukoplakia is a precancerous lesion. Management: cessation of risk factors (smoking, tobacco, alcohol). Biopsy of suspicious lesions. Surgical excision if dysplasia. Regular follow-up (every 3-6 months). Free oral cancer screening at government hospitals.
precautions: Stop all tobacco and alcohol use
Regular dental/oral medicine checkups
If lesion changes (redness, ulceration, induration), biopsy urgently
Maintain good oral hygiene
Avoid irritants

symptoms: non-healing ulcer or growth in the mouth
guidance: Oral cancer is common in India. Early detection saves lives—free oral cancer screening at PHCs under National Cancer Screening Programme. Treatment: surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy—free at government hospitals under PMJAY. Prevention: avoid tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol.
precautions: Stop tobacco, areca nut, and alcohol
Get oral screening at every health visit
If ulcer does not heal in 2 weeks, seek biopsy
If a lump in the neck, get evaluated
HPV vaccine (for oropharyngeal cancer prevention)
